digo_source: Mgombato ('mnazi coconut tree'; 'nazi coconut'); ICRAF ('Digo: Mnazi'); Pakia 2005

teaser.en: The Digo have a name for every stage of a coconut, from the tiny *kolokotsi* to the overripe *nguta*: seven in all.

summary.en: *Mnazi*, the coconut palm, grows on almost every Digo homestead and is the backbone of coastal cooking, building and income. Kwale and Kilifi hold most of Kenya's coconut trees, and from milk to thatch to palm wine, few plants matter more to Digo life.

about.en:
*Mnazi* is a tall, slender palm, up to 20 metres, with a single trunk that often leans or curves, topped by a crown of long feathery fronds. The fruits hang in bunches below the leaves, and the Digo have a name for each stage of their growth. Pakia records seven: *kolokotsi*, *tale*, *daka*, *dafu* (the young drinking nut), *koroma*, *nazi* (the mature nut) and *nguta* (overripe).

Pakia also records three Digo kinds of coconut palm, told apart by the colour of their nuts: *mnazi mwiru*, dark green; *mnazi wa kundu*, orange; and *mnazi wa chisamli*, yellow.

where.en: Coconut palms grow on almost every Digo homestead and in groves inland of Diani and Msambweni. Kwale and Kilifi counties hold most of Kenya's coconut trees, and the palm-lined coast is the signature of Digo country.

uses.en:
Coconut is in nearly everything the Digo cook. Grated *nazi* is squeezed through the *chifumbu*, a woven basket strainer, to give *huwi* or *uwi*, coconut milk, which goes into rice, cassava, fish, beans and greens. The leftover dregs are *dindiya*, and grated coconut also makes *kashata*, a coconut sweet. The young *dafu* is drunk straight from the nut.

The palm is also tapped for palm wine, *uchi* or *tembo*. The tapper, the *mjema*, climbs to the crown and taps the *phalanga* to collect the sap.

Almost nothing goes to waste. Fronds (*kuti*, plural *makuti*) are used for thatch, and woven fronds are *makandza*. Leaves are made into *hundu* baskets, strips of *mkpwuna* serve as twine, coir is twisted into *ndifu* rope, and the shells, *chivo*, become ladles and fuel. The trunk is used as timber. Coconuts and their products are a major source of income on the coast.

culture.en: The Mgombato dictionary records two proverbs. *Mnazi mmwenga una uchi wani?* asks 'How much palm wine can you get from one palm tree?' *Mnazi wa mchetu taujemwa na ndaro* says 'Your wife's coconut palm is not tapped joyfully', because it still belongs to her. Palm wine is woven into coastal social life, and in a mostly Muslim community it is also a lived tension.

names.en: The Digo name is *mnazi*, and the nut is *nazi*; both are shared with Swahili and Giriama. The names are recorded in the Mgombato dictionary, the ICRAF handbook and Pakia. In English it is the coconut palm, and its scientific name is *Cocos nucifera*, from *nucifera*, 'nut-bearing'.

conservation.en: Groves have been lost to titanium mining, and many trees are ageing; replanting programmes aim to renew them.

reason.en: Another palm tapped for palm wine
Also tapped for palm wine and used for thatch and weaving
Rice is cooked in coconut milk
Cassava is cooked in coconut milk
Cashew, the other great tree cash crop of the coast

definition.en: The leaf of the coconut palm. Leaves in general are makodza, but the coconut leaf has its own name; kuti is used less for other feather-leaved palms (Phoenix, Raphia) and never for cycads. Mgombato also uses kuti for roofing thatch made from palm leaves.

use.en: Plaited roofing (vyungo), woven mats (kandza) and brooms (liphyero) are made from it; Pakia says those made from other palms are of poorer quality.

definition.en: The woody midrib that runs the length of the coconut leaf. Mgombato spells it bati (class ma): 'wooden stem of palm leaf'.

use.en: Used to make vyungo (fronds are tied back onto it to make thatch) and mbano, sticks for smoking fish.

definition.en: The thick stalk at the base of the coconut leaf, where it joins the trunk. Mgombato describes it as the part of the branch nearest the trunk.

use.en: Burned as firewood, especially by commercial food vendors; Mgombato adds that it is often used as an improvised seat.

shared_with: kumbi: the outer skin of the coconut fruit

definition.en: The leaflets of the coconut leaf, the long narrow blades along the midrib. Pakia says makalala and mikalala are interchangeable.

meaning.en: Probably named after the rustling noise the leaflets make in the wind.

definition.en: The thin midrib of each coconut leaflet. When the word is used for another palm a phrase is added, as in ukuti wa uchindu, which shows the coconut is the model for these names.

use.en: Bundled into brooms (liphyero) and made into fish traps (tsatsa).

definition.en: One frond (leaflet) of a palm leaf. Mgombato gives its plural as kuti and its Swahili as ukuti; it may be related to Pakia's ukuti, which Pakia defines as the leaflet's midrib.
The fibrous material on the coconut leaf stalk; Mgombato describes it as the fibres that hold a frond to the palm. The same word names the coir of the fruit.

use.en: Used as a sieve, especially when tapping palm sap.

shared_with: ndifu: the coir (fibrous husk) of the coconut fruit

definition.en: A coconut frond, and a mat woven from one. Mgombato also lists likandza (plural makandza), a woven palm frond used as a mat.
The tender, edible part at the top of the coconut palm (or raffia palm) between the stem and the leaves.
The flowering branch of the coconut palm, the part that develops into coconuts.

meaning.en: The word also means 'to sow'; Pakia found no clear link between the two.

definition.en: The small flowers (florets) on the coconut flower branch. In Pakia's sequence the fruit develops from punga, before the kolokotsi stage.

meaning.en: Named for their likeness to the rice panicle, mphunga.

shared_with: punga: the male tassel of maize
punga: the flowering panicles of grasses and sugarcane

definition.en: The stalks of the coconut flower branch that carry the fruits. Mgombato: the part of the palm that holds the coconuts.
The cover that wraps the coconut flower branch. Mgombato adds that palm wine is tapped from this part.

use.en: Burned as firewood; tapped for palm wine.

definition.en: The first stage of the coconut, very small, with no water or flesh inside. Mgombato: little more than a bud and not yet edible.
The second stage: still immature and small, but larger than kolokotsi, with hardly any water or flesh.

use.en: Also used only for magic-related purposes.

definition.en: The third stage: still immature but now large, with some water that is not yet sweet and no flesh.
The middle stage: the water is sweet and there is a thin layer of soft flesh.
The stage between dafu and nazi: the water is no longer sweet and the flesh is too hard to enjoy fresh, but still too soft to make coconut milk (uwi).
The mature coconut, the most useful stage. Nazi is also the everyday word for any coconut, but strictly it means this stage.

use.en: Grated to make coconut milk (uwi) for cooking and for making coconut oil; the Digo grow coconut palms mainly for the nazi.

definition.en: A late, over-mature stage that farmers mostly avoid.

use.en: The flesh is chewed and is believed to be an aphrodisiac; it can also be sold as copra for oil.

definition.en: The outer skin of the coconut fruit. The same word names the base of the leaf stalk.

shared_with: kumbi: the base of the coconut leaf stalk

definition.en: The coir, the fibrous layer of the coconut husk. The same word names the fibres on the leaf stalk.

use.en: The coir husk is used for scrubbing utensils, like steel wool; more recently it is made into floor rags and processed into coco-peat for potting soil.

shared_with: ndifu: the fibres on the coconut leaf stalk

definition.en: The husk, the whole outer covering of the coconut.

use.en: Used for firewood, for stuffing mattresses and for making rope.

definition.en: The hard inner shell of the coconut.

use.en: Used as fuel; Mgombato adds ladles, and Pakia notes it is now also made into bracelets.

definition.en: The empty shell of a young coconut (dafu).
The clear liquid inside the coconut. Pakia stresses that this, not uwi, is what English calls 'coconut water' or sometimes 'coconut milk'.
The white flesh of the coconut, the part grated for coconut milk.

shared_with: nazi: the mature stage of the fruit, and the coconut in general

definition.en: The soft, edible flesh of a young drinking coconut (dafu).
The embryo inside the coconut, from which the new palm grows.

meaning.en: Moon; Pakia suggests the round embryo looks like a full moon.

shared_with: mwezi: the cotyledon of the mango seed

definition.en: The three 'eyes' (scars) on the coconut shell; the same word is used for a bean's hilum and a potato's eye buds.
Coconuts tied together in a bunch.
A bunch of coconuts still on their fruit stalks.
Coconut milk: the creamy liquid squeezed from grated mature coconut (nazi). Mgombato spells it huwi and describes straining the grated pulp with water through a chifumbu basket.

use.en: Used for cooking and for making coconut oil.

definition.en: The coconut left in the shell after grating.
Palm wine tapped from the coconut palm.
Palm wine; also liquor, beer or any alcoholic drink.
A section of thatch made from coconut leaves: leaflets are plucked and tied one by one back onto the midrib (mbati), overlapping so that rain cannot get through.

use.en: Roofing. Mgombato: viungo vya mwenga mwenga is a single layer of thatch, viungo vya mairi mairi a double layer.

definition.en: A strip of palm leaf, for example for tying leaves onto a stick to make sections of thatch. Mgombato does not name the palm; its plural ng'ongo is also a separate raffia word.
A strip of coconut frond used as string or twine.
A broom; Pakia names it among the things made from the leaflet midribs (mikuti).
A fish trap made from the leaflet midribs (mikuti).
Sticks for smoking fish, made from the leaf midrib (mbati).

mgombato: mnazi (mi) coconut tree (Cocos nucifera); mnazi. Proverb: Mnazi mmwenga una uchi wani? How much palm wine can you get from one palm tree?; Proverb: Mnazi wa mchetu taujemwa na ndaro. Your wife's coconut palm is not tapped joyfully (because it still belongs to her).
